title: BCM Rule
intro: The Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) rule (1982) is a rate-based learning law, older than STDP, that solved a problem plain Hebbian learning cannot: stability. A synapse potentiates when the postsynaptic rate is above a threshold and depresses when it is below, and the threshold itself slides with the neuron's recent average activity. Too much activity raises the bar and too little lowers it, so learning is selective and self-stabilizing at the same time.

blocks.source:
dw_i/dt = eta * x_i * phi(y, theta_M)
phi(y, theta_M) = y (y - theta_M)              the simplest choice of phi
theta_M = <y^2> / y_0                          sliding modification threshold: a running average of y^2

x_i: presynaptic rate, y: postsynaptic rate

items: If y > theta_M, active inputs potentiate (LTP). If 0 < y < theta_M, active inputs depress (LTD). Inactive inputs (x_i = 0) do not change.

Because theta_M grows faster than the mean rate (it tracks y squared), a neuron that becomes very responsive raises its own threshold until most inputs depress. A neuron that falls silent lowers it until inputs can potentiate again. This is metaplasticity: plasticity of plasticity.

Under this rule, a neuron becomes selective. It ends up responding strongly to one input pattern (or a few) and weakly to the rest, which is how BCM explains the development of orientation selectivity and ocular dominance in visual cortex.

config.yLabel: φ(y, θ_M), weight change per unit input

blocks.text: What to read off the plot

Each curve is phi(y) for a neuron with a different recent history: half, equal to and one and a half times the chosen average activity. Where a curve crosses zero is theta_M. Higher average activity moves the crossing to the right and deepens the LTD region: the same input that would have caused LTP in a quiet neuron causes LTD in an active one. Slide the average up and watch the threshold move faster than linearly, because it follows y squared.

items: Monocular deprivation. Closing one eye shifts cortical responses toward the open eye. BCM explains the loss as LTD of the deprived eye's inputs, driven by noisy activity that falls below theta_M. In line with that, lid suture, which leaves noisy retinal activity, depresses deprived-eye responses more than silencing the retina with TTX (Rittenhouse, Shouval, Paradiso & Bear 1999).

LTD/LTP crossover. In hippocampal area CA1, 900 pulses at 1-3 Hz induce LTD, the same number at 50 Hz induces LTP, and around 10 Hz there is little change (Dudek & Bear 1992). That is the shape of phi: depression below a crossover rate, potentiation above it.

A threshold that slides. In slices of visual cortex from dark-reared rats, which have had low average activity, LTP is larger and LTD smaller across stimulation frequencies, so the crossover has moved down; two days of light exposure moves it back (Kirkwood, Rioult & Bear 1996). This, not the 1992 frequency curve, is the direct evidence for a sliding theta_M.
Molecular basis. Changes in NMDA receptor subunit composition (NR2A vs NR2B) after altered visual experience are one proposed mechanism for the moving threshold.

blocks.text: BCM and STDP are not rivals. Izhikevich and Desai (2003) showed that pair-based STDP with nearest-neighbor spike interactions produces BCM-like rate dependence. Pfister and Gerstner (2006) showed that the triplet STDP rule averages to a BCM rule when its pair-depression amplitude is made to depend on the neuron's mean rate: the sliding threshold falls out of spike-timing plasticity plus homeostasis. Clopath et al.'s voltage rule has the same two-threshold shape with voltage in place of rate. See #/snn/learning-rules/stdp-triplet and #/snn/learning-rules/stdp-voltage.
The threshold must adapt faster than the weights (tauTheta of seconds to minutes against much slower learning). Otherwise the rule oscillates.

For a cortical column: BCM's sliding threshold is a template for homeostasis in your column. Whatever spike-based rule you use for feedforward feature learning, add a per-neuron threshold that tracks recent activity. It keeps every cell in a useful range and pushes different cells toward different input patterns, which is the sparse, specialized code minicolumns rely on.
